guidance.summary: On a schedule you have defined (at least annually) you check every one of the 110 requirements to see whether it is actually working the way your SSP says - not just whether a policy exists. The assessment can be done by you, the MSP or an outside firm, but it must be written down, cover each requirement using the 800-171A objectives, and produce findings that go into the POA&M. This is the periodic deep check; 3.12.3 is the continuous watching in between.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Policy requires a full self-assessment against NIST SP 800-171A every 12 months and a targeted assessment after major changes. Each September the IT admin and the MSP walk through all 110 requirements using the 800-171A objectives: examining artifacts, interviewing the office manager and shop supervisor, and testing settings (trying a blocked USB stick, checking MFA on a test account, attempting a restore). Results are recorded per objective (met, not met, not applicable) in the assessment workbook, the SPRS score is recalculated and resubmitted, and every 'not met' goes to the POA&M with an owner and date.
typical_evidence: Assessment policy or SSP section defining frequency and method
Completed assessment workbook or report with date, assessor, per-objective results and evidence references
Prior assessment reports showing the cycle is being followed
SPRS submission record consistent with the assessment
POA&M entries created from assessment findings
Third-party or MSP assessment engagement letter, if used
common_gaps: The SPRS self-score was entered once years ago and never revisited
The assessment is a checklist of 'do we have a policy' with no testing of whether controls work
Findings noted but never turned into POA&M items
remediation_steps: Write the assessment policy: full assessment of all 110 requirements at least annually, targeted reassessment after significant changes, who performs it, and how results are recorded.
Build an assessment workbook with every 800-171A objective (320 objectives) and columns for status, evidence location and notes.
Perform the assessment using examine, interview and test methods, and collect evidence artifacts into an organized evidence folder per control.
Record findings, update the SSP where actual implementation differs from what was written, and create POA&M items for every unmet objective with owner and due date.
Recalculate and resubmit the SPRS score within 30 days of completing the assessment, and calendar the next one.

guidance.summary: Every requirement you have not fully met, and every significant weakness found by assessments, scans or incidents, goes onto a plan of action and milestones (POA&M) that says what is wrong, what you will do about it, who owns it, what resources it needs and when it will be done. Then you work the plan and update it as items close. A POA&M that never changes is a sign it is not being implemented.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop keeps a POA&M spreadsheet with one row per open item, for example: '3.13.11 - backup encryption not FIPS-validated; action: move to the backup product's FIPS mode; owner: IT admin; resources: $2,400 license; milestones: quote by Oct 15, deploy by Nov 30; status: in progress.' Items come from the annual assessment, the monthly scans and the incident log. The owner and IT review it monthly, close items with a link to the evidence, and keep closed rows in a history tab. The assessor can see items opened, worked and closed across the past year.
typical_evidence: Current POA&M with weakness, source, planned actions, owner, resources, milestones with dates, and status
POA&M history showing items closed with dates and evidence references
Monthly review meeting notes or tickets showing progress
Assessment report, scan reports or incident records that fed the POA&M
POA&M template consistent with the NIST CUI POA&M format
common_gaps: No POA&M, or one created for the SPRS submission and never touched again
Items with no owner, date or resources, so nothing ever moves
Only assessment findings tracked; scan results and incident lessons never make it in
remediation_steps: Adopt a POA&M template with columns for control ID, weakness description, source (assessment, scan, incident), planned actions, owner, resources needed, milestones and dates, status, completion date and evidence.
Populate it from the latest self-assessment, the last vulnerability scan and the risk assessment, including every requirement that is not fully implemented.
Assign an owner and realistic dates to each item (a CMMC conditional certification allows 180 days for POA&M closeout, so plan tighter than that).
Review the POA&M monthly with the owner: update status, reallocate resources, and close items only with evidence attached.
Keep closed items in a history tab and reference the POA&M from the SSP.

guidance.summary: Between annual assessments you continuously check that key controls still work: reviewing logs and alerts, confirming patches applied, checking backup success, reviewing account and access lists, verifying MFA and encryption status, watching scan trends. You should have a written monitoring schedule (what is checked, how often, by whom) and records showing the checks happened. This is what keeps controls from quietly decaying between assessments.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's continuous monitoring plan is a one-page table: daily - EDR and backup job alerts reviewed by IT; weekly - patch compliance report and firewall alerts; monthly - vulnerability scan review, review of new and disabled accounts, USB block log, physical access logs; quarterly - full access recertification, BitLocker and MFA status export, restore test, POA&M review; annually - full assessment, policy review, training. Each check is a recurring ticket in the MSP's system that is closed with a note or screenshot, so a year of evidence accumulates on its own.
typical_evidence: Continuous monitoring plan or schedule listing controls, what is checked, frequency and owner
Recurring ticket or checklist history showing checks were performed on schedule
Dashboards or reports used: EDR, patch compliance, backup success, MFA coverage, scan trends
Quarterly access review records
Evidence that a monitoring finding led to a fix (ticket or POA&M item)
common_gaps: Controls set up once and never checked; MFA quietly disabled for a user, backups failing for months
Alerts go to a mailbox nobody reads
No schedule, so monitoring is whatever the MSP happens to notice
Monitoring happens but leaves no record
remediation_steps: Write a monitoring schedule that maps each key control to a check, a frequency and an owner (daily alerts, weekly patch and backup status, monthly scan, account and log reviews, quarterly recertification and restore tests, annual assessment).
Turn on the dashboards and reports the checks depend on (EDR, RMM patch compliance, backup job status, Entra ID or AD MFA and sign-in reports, scanner trends) and route alerts to a monitored queue.
Create recurring tickets or a checklist for each check and require a note or screenshot when it is closed.
Feed any failure into the incident process or the POA&M and record the fix.
Review the monitoring records quarterly with the owner and adjust the schedule after each annual assessment.

guidance.summary: The SSP is the master document describing your CUI environment: what is in scope (the boundary), what the environment looks like (hardware, software, network, cloud services, locations, people), how each of the 110 requirements is implemented or why it is not applicable and who approved that, and what other systems you connect to (GCC High, the MSP's tools, customer portals). You define how often it is updated - at least annually and after major changes - and you keep it current. Without an SSP a DoD assessment cannot be scored at all, which is why the requirement carries no point value.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's SSP is a 60-page document: a scope section with a network diagram showing the CUI VLAN (25 PCs, file server, 2 CNC controllers, firewall), the GCC High tenant, the MSP's remote-management connection and the out-of-scope guest Wi-Fi; an asset list; a table of people and roles; and, for each of the 110 requirements, a paragraph stating how it is implemented and pointing to the policy or setting. The one requirement marked not applicable (3.13.14, because the shop has no VoIP) carries the owner's signed approval. The version table shows annual updates each September and an extra update after the GCC High migration.
typical_evidence: The SSP itself, with version history, approval signature and date
Network or boundary diagram and asset inventory referenced by the SSP
Per-requirement implementation statements covering all 110 requirements
Signed not-applicable determinations by the designated authority (the owner)
Interconnection list or agreements for external systems (GCC High, MSP, customer portals)
Policy or SSP clause defining the update frequency and evidence of updates
common_gaps: No SSP, or a generic template with the vendor's name still in it
Boundary not defined, so the assessor cannot tell whether the shop-floor controllers or the guest Wi-Fi are in scope
Implementation statements that just restate the requirement ('the organization limits access') instead of describing what is actually done
Not-applicable decisions made by IT with no documented approval, and the SSP never updated since it was first written
remediation_steps: Start from the NIST CUI SSP template and set the boundary: list every asset that stores, processes or transmits CUI, the security-protection assets (firewall, EDR, backup), and what is out of scope; draw the network diagram.
Describe the environment of operation: locations, hardware, software, cloud services, users and roles, and the CUI data flow from customer receipt to delivery.

For each of the 110 requirements write a specific implementation statement (what, where, who, which setting or policy) and mark its status (implemented, partially implemented, planned, not applicable).
Document each not-applicable determination with a rationale and the owner's signature as the designated authority.
List external connections (GCC High, MSP remote management, customer portals, email gateway) and how each is protected or covered by agreement.
Set the update frequency in the SSP (annually and after significant change), maintain a version table, and have the owner approve each version.
